text: You've seen the T-account shape already, in passing. This lesson slows down and actually uses one, posting real transactions and finding a balance.

A T-account has three parts: the account name on top, debits on the left, credits on the right. To post a transaction, you write the dollar amount on the correct side. An increase to a debit-normal account, like cash, goes on the left; a decrease goes on the right.

Picture a fictional company, Brightwell Logistics. The owner invests ten thousand cash. It pays two thousand rent. It receives forty-five hundred from a customer. It pays eight hundred for fuel. Posting only the cash account: debits of ten thousand and forty-five hundred on the left, credits of two thousand and eight hundred on the right.

To find the balance, total each side and subtract the smaller from the larger. Total debits: fourteen thousand five hundred. Total credits: twenty-eight hundred. The difference, eleven thousand seven hundred, is a debit balance - which makes sense, because cash is an asset, and assets are debit-normal.

When you later drill into an account balance inside Oracle Fusion General Ledger, you're looking at exactly this: a running total of debits and credits, netted down to a balance. The screen is modern; the arithmetic underneath is this T-account math. Up next, lesson seven: recording a transaction step by step.
